Learning to predict the next word offered a way to learn the patterns of language. So, a team at Google built a new architecture around attention. It could learn which earlier words mattered and pay more attention to them when predicting the next one. The Transformer was born: a mathematical structure that could learn from vast collections of text. In this series, we will learn how predicting the next word leads to agentic systems doing a job. Learn how this technology matured over nearly a decade, and build an intuitive understanding of how to use it.

variants.title: Build the project around the problem
variants.text:
Before we dive in, here’s what we’ll cover.

First, we’ll build a useful mental model. Computers work with numbers; we’ll use directions to picture how those numbers can represent relationships between words.

With that picture, we’ll see how language models learn from text, and how context shapes their next prediction. Think of this as a text calculator, working out what might follow.

Next comes the assistant. In a conversation such as ChatGPT, a user asks and the model continues as the assistant. Training helps it follow requests; instructions behind the conversation shape its response.

From there, we’ll see how an answer leads to an action. The harness parses tool requests from the model’s output, runs permitted operations, and brings the results back into context.

With that loop, we can build a project around a problem: a brief, sources, drafts and checks. The agent can read, edit and organize these files, carrying useful work beyond the chat.

And those same file skills can improve the agent’s guidance. We’ll turn lessons from the work into instructions, saved memory, reusable skills and hooks, then check what changes in the next run.

Let’s start with words, numbers and directions.

variants.title: Geometry-led discovery
variants.text:
Computers work with numbers. Words carry meaning. So how could a collection of numbers help a computer work with something like language? Let’s build a picture, one step at a time.

Try the simplest idea: give every word a number. Put cat, dog, car, fish and boat along a line. Now each word has a label and a place.

But hold on. If cat is one and car is two, does that make their meanings neighbours? Would moving dog farther away make it less like cat? The numbering alone has told us nothing about those relationships.

The labels can still identify the words. What we need is a richer representation behind them, one that can capture useful relationships. What happens if we give each word two numbers instead?

Now we have a map. One number moves a point across it; another moves it up or down. We can put related words near one another and leave room for other relationships. But we have to choose useful positions. Random dots would not solve the problem.

Draw an arrow from the same starting point to each word. Every arrow points somewhere. For this mental picture, let’s focus on those directions: similar, different, or opposite. The real calculation can use length as well.

Let’s invent two features for our drawing: living or built, and land or water. Cat and dog can share a region. Fish shares one relationship with them, and another with boat. Already, the map is doing more than a numbered list.

Here’s the catch. The plane has many possible directions, but only two independent axes. Suppose we also want a separate way to distinguish small from large. We can mix that into our map, or give it another coordinate.

With a third number, the map opens into space. Now we can change that third feature while keeping the first two in place. Related words can form clusters, and the same word can combine several features.

So why stop at three? Language carries far more relationships than our little drawing. A model can use hundreds or thousands of coordinates. It learns useful patterns from examples of language; it is not handed our tidy, named axes.

Those learned relationships can overlap. There is no requirement for every meaning to have its own private axis. Our drawing gives us an intuition: many numbers can describe a much richer pattern than one arbitrary label.

Keep that picture: words represented by numbers, pictured as directions in a richer space. Next, we’ll see how the words around a word can change its representation, and how that helps a language model predict what comes next.

variants.label: B
variants.title: Build a word map together
variants.text:
Let’s try a small challenge. Build a map for five words: cat, dog, fish, car and boat. A computer needs numbers, so the first question is simple: what should those numbers tell it?

Give each word a number and place it on a line. That gets us started. But now the map says some words are bigger, smaller, nearer or farther apart. Did we learn anything about meaning, or only about the labels we chose?

Imagine cat sitting next to car, with dog at the far end. The numbers are perfectly good labels. They just haven’t captured the relationship we wanted. So let’s ask for something more useful: keep related words together.

Give each word two coordinates. Now our line becomes a plane, and there are many more ways to arrange the words. Cat and dog can share a neighbourhood; car and boat can share another. That feels like a better start.

But boat has something in common with fish, too. A useful map should carry more than one relationship at once. For our drawing, try living versus built across one axis, and land versus water across the other.

Now draw arrows from a shared starting point. The direction toward fish combines features from our two axes. We can picture related meanings through related directions. That is the lens we’ll use here; it doesn’t mean length is irrelevant to the real model.

There are plenty of directions on this plane. The limit is subtler: only two coordinates can vary independently. Suppose we want to describe another feature without changing the two we already chose. We need another independent control.

So add a third coordinate. The plane opens into a space we can look around. A small animal and a large animal can share some relationships while differing in another. Groups become clusters, with differences still visible inside them.

Three helps, but it is still our tiny drawing. Think of all the ways words can be related: use, subject, tone, and the context around them. Why try to squeeze that richness into the three dimensions we can easily draw?

Language models can learn representations with hundreds or thousands of numbers. The model learns the arrangement from language. Our named axes were a teaching aid; real learned relationships can overlap and do not each need their own perpendicular axis.

That is the discovery we needed. One number can identify a word. A learned collection of numbers can represent a richer pattern of relationships, and directions give us a way to picture it.

We’ll keep using this picture as the story develops. First, what happens when a word meets the words around it? That brings us to context, and to the next-word prediction at the heart of a language model.

variants.text:
Keep the direction picture in mind. A river bank and a savings bank use the same word, but the surrounding words point toward different meanings.

Where did those relationships come from? During training, existing text supplies a beginning and the next piece that actually followed it. The model’s prediction is compared with that example, and its learned numbers are adjusted. Across many examples, this builds a model of language.

Using the trained model is a different step. A partly filled context window supplies the material for a continuation. Attention lets information from earlier words shape the internal representation. In our picture, the directions change.

From that representation, the model assigns probabilities to possible next tokens: pieces of text that can be words or parts of words. After “the river bank was,” different continuations fit than after “the savings bank was.” Flooded might fit the first; closed, the second.

One token is selected and added to the context. What was output becomes part of the next input. Repeat, and a sentence can grow into a page.

That gives us the autocomplete engine. Changing its current context does not itself retrain it. But relevant facts, examples, constraints and work already done can shape what follows. Building that context is part of doing the job.

But a convincing continuation doesn’t necessarily follow a request. What happens when that same engine is trained to follow instructions, then given a role in a conversation?

variants.text:
The river bank was… What might come next? Flooded would fit one continuation. Now change the context: the savings bank was… Closed might fit. The earlier words change which continuations make sense.

Inside a language model, the earlier words are represented by numbers. Attention helps combine information from relevant positions. Through our direction picture, imagine the context reshaping those representations before the next prediction is made.

The result is a set of probabilities for what comes next. The pieces are called tokens: sometimes a whole word, sometimes part of one. A token is chosen, added to the context, and the model predicts again. Repeating that loop produces a passage.

Where did that ability come from? During training, examples of language supply both a partial passage and what actually followed. Comparing a prediction with that next piece gives a learning signal that adjusts the model’s numbers, over many examples.

Using the trained model is different. The context window holds the material available for this continuation. Adding a fact or an example can change the answer without retraining the model. That is why choosing the right context matters so much.

So think beyond a chat partner. This is an engine for continuing a partly filled context. We can supply a goal, evidence and examples, then evaluate what follows. Making it reliably respond to a request required another step: instruction-following and the assistant role.

variants.text:
Completing a passage is useful. But if someone asks for a clear explanation, the desired result is an answer that follows the request, not simply more text in the same style.

Researchers trained models on examples of helpful responses, then used human feedback to shape that behaviour further. The goal was to make following a user’s intent more likely.

The context was also organized into roles. A user supplies a request; the model is prompted to continue as the assistant. ChatGPT, released in 2022, brought this exchange to a public chat interface.

The conversation on screen is only part of what the model receives. The application can place system instructions alongside the visible turns, shaping how the response should be produced.

In our direction picture, these instructions help steer the continuation. The model is still working from supplied material, but that material now includes guidance about how to respond.

Users can supply clearer goals, relevant material, corrections and examples. Some controls come from the application. So the useful skill is learning what can be shaped through the context—and what remains outside the user’s control.

Now the model can help in a directed conversation. Yet asking it to check a file does not itself read that file. Something outside the model has to carry out the action.

That works for code, but also for research notes, lesson plans and video projects. The important step is representing enough of the problem as files the system can work with.

The files remain between sessions. The model sees what is read or otherwise supplied to its current context, not everything on disk at once. Relevant work can be brought back when the next step needs it.

That means project design matters. A clear brief, useful references, linked drafts and recorded decisions make the next step easier. Files can hold both the deliverable and the context needed to create it.

The practical utility is help building and operating a file-based representation of a problem. The person chooses the goal, reviews the work and decides what counts as done. Chat becomes one surface for working with that project.

experiment.question: Which explains durable control better: A introduces mechanisms; B repairs one repeated mistake?
experiment.A: Current guide1: operating files → hooks → example → improvement.
experiment.B: A repeated audience mismatch motivates saved guidance, deliberate loading, an event check and verified repair.
experiment.decision: Choose mechanism-first or failure-and-repair story; keep human authority and model weights distinct.

variants.label: A
variants.title: Current guide1: operating files → hooks → example → improvement.
variants.text:
The project folder can hold more than results. It can also hold instructions, saved memory and the code that controls how work proceeds. The same file tools can help maintain those operating files.

A written instruction still depends on the model using it correctly. A lifecycle hook adds a defined point where the surrounding software can do something whenever a chosen event occurs.

That could be before an action, after a result, or before the system stops. A hook can run a check, collect evidence or load relevant memory. What it can intercept depends on the application.

For example, before exporting this video, a programmed check could require the manuscript review to be complete. If it is not, the export waits. The model does not have to remember that rule each time.

Experience from the work can then feed another loop: notice a problem, propose a change to the guidance or harness, review it, and verify what the next run actually does.

Instructions and memory can be read into later context. Hook code can make chosen checks repeatable. These changes live in the surrounding system; they do not retrain the underlying model’s weights.

The useful whole is now visible: a language model, the context it receives, actions performed through tools, persistent project files, and controls directed by people.

Learning to build that environment gives people a practical way to extend their work: represent their problems, retain lessons, and cultivate a digital extension they can inspect, steer and improve.

variants.label: B
variants.title: A repeated audience mismatch motivates saved guidance, deliberate loading, an event check and verified repair.
variants.text:
The next draft misses the audience again. Writing the same reminder in every chat is a fragile solution. Instead, the project can retain the lesson in a guidance file: who this video is for, what went wrong, and how to check the next draft.

That file helps only when its contents reach the model. The harness can read relevant instructions and saved memory into the context at the right time. In our direction picture, the next continuation now starts with that guidance included.

But an instruction still depends on the model following it. A hook adds an event-driven step in the surrounding software. Before an action, after a result, or at another supported lifecycle event, it can run a check or supply context.

For this video, imagine an export check that requires the manuscript review to be complete. If the review is missing, the export waits. That rule is implemented in software; it does not depend on the model remembering a sentence.

The agent’s file skills can help improve these instructions and checks, too. Notice a failure, propose a repair, review the change, then test the next run. The person retains authority over what changes and whether it worked.

This is improvement in the environment around the model, not retraining of its weights. The whole system combines a language model, assembled context, tools, persistent files and human-directed controls.

Learning to build that environment is a path toward becoming an independent operator: someone who can represent a problem, retain useful experience, and steer a digital extension of their work. Its value comes from what it helps people do, and from keeping the work open to inspection and correction.
